items.title: Ministers and civil servants working together (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK, About the Civil Service; Civil Service Code
items.body: Ministers and civil servants have different jobs, and the system works because each does their own. Ministers are politicians. They were elected by the public, or appointed to the House of Lords, and they decide the policies of the government. They answer to Parliament and to voters for what their department does. Civil servants are not elected and do not take a side in politics. Their job is to give ministers honest advice and then carry out the decisions that ministers make. If a minister wants to do something, a civil servant should explain the options, the costs and the likely effects, even if the news is unwelcome. Once the minister has decided, the civil servant puts the decision into action, even if they might have chosen differently. A civil servant does not refuse to carry out a lawful decision because they disagree with it. Civil servants also stay when governments change. This is why they must work equally well for ministers from different parties. Ministers can be replaced after an election or a reshuffle, but the civil servants provide continuity, which means the department's knowledge, systems and services keep going. A good relationship between ministers and civil servants depends on trust. Ministers need to trust that advice is honest. Civil servants need to trust that ministers will take it seriously.

questions.prompt: Why do ministers have to answer to Parliament for what their department does?

options.text: They choose which civil servants are promoted within the department
They carry out the department's daily work themselves
They are the most senior civil servants in the department
They are the politicians who take the department's decisions

questions.hint: Ministers take the decisions, so they are held to account for them.

questions.prompt: A minister's favoured plan will cost more than first expected. What should a civil servant do?

options.text: Share the figures with the Opposition to test opinion
Mention the cost only after the plan is announced
Tell the minister the real cost, even though it is unwelcome
Leave the cost out of the briefing so that the plan is not delayed

questions.hint: Honest advice is needed even when it is unwelcome.

questions.prompt: After a minister has made a lawful decision, what should a civil servant do?

options.text: Put it into action, even if they would have chosen differently
Delay it until after the next general election
Ask Parliament to vote on the decision before any action is taken
Refuse to act on it if they personally disagree with it

questions.hint: Civil servants carry out lawful decisions once they are made.

questions.prompt: What does continuity mean when a government changes?

options.text: All the senior civil servants swap departments
The department pauses until new ministers arrive
The new ministers are required to keep all the old policies
The department's knowledge and services keep going

questions.hint: Civil servants stay in post so the department keeps running.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a civil servant's role towards ministers?

options.text: They advise ministers, then carry out their decisions
They choose the policy, then ministers carry it out
They appoint the ministers who lead their department
They check each decision for Parliament before it is made

questions.hint: Ministers decide; civil servants advise and deliver.

questions.prompt: Why must civil servants serve ministers of any party equally well?

options.text: They are chosen by whichever party is in power
They move departments whenever the governing party changes
Ministers from every party sit in each department
The party in government can change after an election

questions.hint: Governments change, so civil servants must serve any of them.

questions.prompt: What does a good working relationship between ministers and civil servants depend on?

options.text: Civil servants having worked earlier as ministers
Trust that advice is honest and taken seriously
Telling ministers in advance what they want to hear
Agreement about which party is best for the country

questions.hint: Trust has to run in both directions.

questions.prompt: Who answers MPs' questions in the House of Commons about a department's policy?

options.text: The minister who leads the department
The chief executive of one of its agencies
The Cabinet Secretary
The department's Permanent Secretary

questions.hint: Ministers, not civil servants, answer for policy in the Commons.

items.title: Political impartiality in everyday life (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code
items.body: Political impartiality means that civil servants do not let their own political views affect the way they do their work. A civil servant may have private opinions, but at work they must serve the government of the day equally, whichever party is in power. This is one of the four values in the Civil Service Code. Impartiality also covers how civil servants behave outside work. They should not use official time, equipment or information for party political purposes. For example, a civil servant must not use their work email to send out campaign messages. There are rules about political activity, and they are stricter for more senior staff, because they work closer to ministers. Anyone who wants to stand for election or take an active part in a party should check the rules with their manager or HR first. Civil servants must also be careful on social media. Posting angry or one-sided political comments, especially where people know you work for a department, could make people doubt your impartiality. Impartiality also means treating customers fairly. A decision on a claim must be made on the facts and the rules, not on whether you like the person, their opinions or their background.

questions.prompt: What does political impartiality mean for a civil servant at work?

options.text: Having no private opinions about politics, whether at work or in private life
Refusing to work for ministers who are new to the role
Voting for whichever party currently governs
Serving the government of the day equally, whichever party is in power

questions.hint: Impartiality means personal political views do not affect your work.

questions.prompt: Which of these would break the rule on using official resources for party political purposes?

options.text: Reading a newspaper during the lunch break
Looking up your own payslip on a work computer during a break
Sending campaign messages from a work email account
Attending a team meeting about a new policy

questions.hint: Official equipment must not be used for party politics.

questions.prompt: Why are the political activity rules usually stricter for senior staff?

options.text: They have more influence over public spending only
They work more closely with ministers and policy
They are more likely to be recognised by the public
They have signed more confidentiality agreements

questions.hint: Senior staff work closer to ministers, so impartiality matters more.

questions.prompt: Before standing for election or taking an active role in a party, what should a civil servant do?

options.text: Wait until the party writes to the department
Ask their trade union to agree the plan
Write to the Civil Service Commission for a licence
Check the rules with their manager or HR

questions.hint: The rules vary by role, so check first.

questions.prompt: Why should civil servants be careful about political comments online?

options.text: Any political comment online is against the law for civil servants
Social media companies report political posts to departments
One-sided posts can make people doubt their impartiality
Departments must approve every personal post before it goes up

questions.hint: Public political comments can damage trust in impartiality.

questions.prompt: Which approach is impartial when deciding a customer's claim?

options.text: Deciding quickly to hit the team target
Deciding in favour of customers who are polite
Deciding on the facts and the rules
Deciding in line with what the last customer received

questions.hint: Decisions must be made on the merits of the case.

questions.prompt: In which document is impartiality set out as one of the core values?

options.text: The Ministerial Code
The Official Secrets Act 1989
The Cabinet Manual
The Civil Service Code

questions.hint: Impartiality is one of the four values in the Civil Service Code.

questions.prompt: A new minister from a different party takes over. What shows impartiality?

options.text: Keeping advice to the previous minister's priorities
Giving the same quality of advice as to the last minister
Holding back work until the party's policies are published
Telling the new minister about the old minister's mistakes

questions.hint: Civil servants serve each government equally well.

items.title: Integrity in everyday work (level 2)
items.body: Integrity is the value of putting the obligations of public service above your own interests. In everyday work this means using your position fairly and not for personal gain. The Civil Service Code says that a civil servant should not misuse their official position, for example by using it to gain an advantage for themselves, their family or their friends. It also says civil servants should not accept gifts or hospitality, or any other benefit, that might be seen to influence their judgement. A small gift such as a box of chocolates from a grateful customer is still taken seriously, and you should ask your manager what to do and follow your department's rules. Many departments keep a register of gifts and hospitality. Integrity also means using public money and resources properly. You should not take home office supplies or use a work vehicle for private trips. It means dealing with the public fairly, promptly and with respect, and it means obeying the law. Finally, integrity means being open about a conflict of interest. A conflict of interest is a situation where your personal interests, or those of someone close to you, could affect, or look as if they affect, your work. If you have one, tell your manager, so it can be handled properly.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of misusing an official position?

options.text: Finishing mandatory training before the deadline
Asking a manager about a difficult case
Following the department's guidance on how to assess a claim
Using the job to gain an advantage for a relative

questions.hint: Using a position for personal or family gain breaks the integrity value.

questions.prompt: A grateful customer offers you a box of chocolates. What should you do?

options.text: Refuse it politely without telling your manager or anyone else
Ask your manager and follow the department's rules
Accept it, since it is only a small thank-you
Accept it only if it costs under ten pounds

questions.hint: Gifts that might be seen to influence judgement need careful handling.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a register of gifts and hospitality?

options.text: Listing the gifts a department gives to ministers
Recording customers' complaints about staff
Showing which staff are due for promotion
Keeping an open record of what staff were offered

questions.hint: Registers keep gifts open and transparent.

questions.prompt: Which action shows integrity in the use of public resources?

options.text: Claiming expenses for a journey that was cancelled
Buying equipment from a friend without comparing prices
Using office supplies only for work purposes
Taking spare supplies home for private use

questions.hint: Integrity means using resources only for their proper purpose.

questions.prompt: What is a conflict of interest?

options.text: A public disagreement between two ministers about a department's policy
Personal interests that could affect, or seem to affect, your work
A dispute between civil servants about who does a task
A customer who disagrees with the decision on a claim

questions.hint: Conflicts arise where private interests meet work duties.

questions.prompt: If you have a conflict of interest at work, what should you do?

options.text: Ask the customer to keep quiet about it
Handle it yourself and say nothing unless asked
Pass the case privately to a friendly colleague
Tell your manager so it can be managed properly

questions.hint: Being open lets the conflict be dealt with properly.

questions.prompt: Integrity means putting which of these above your own interests?

options.text: The targets set for your team
The obligations of public service
The instructions of your trade union
The wishes of your closest colleagues

questions.hint: The Code says integrity puts public service first.

questions.prompt: According to the Code, which duty also forms part of integrity?

options.text: Keeping a friend's mistakes private so they avoid trouble
Agreeing with your manager at all times
Complying with the law and upholding justice
Giving polite customers extra priority

questions.hint: The Code requires civil servants to obey the law.

items.title: Honesty in everyday work (level 2)
items.body: Honesty is the value of being truthful and open. The Civil Service Code says that civil servants should set out the facts and relevant issues truthfully, and should correct any errors as soon as they become aware of them. It also says they must not deceive or knowingly mislead ministers, Parliament, or others. In practice, honesty shows up in small ways. If you make a mistake processing a claim, you tell your manager straight away so it can be put right, instead of hoping nobody notices. If a customer asks you something you do not know, you say that you will find out, rather than guessing or inventing an answer. If you are asked to record what happened in a case, you write down what actually happened, and not what would look better. Honesty also applies to the way you describe your work. You must be truthful on timesheets, expenses claims and records of calls. Honesty is vital in the application process too. You must give true information about your employment history and any convictions, because the pre-employment checks will test it, and misleading statements can lead to an offer being withdrawn. Honesty does not mean sharing everything: some information is confidential and you must still protect it. It means never giving a false picture.

questions.prompt: You notice you made a mistake on a claim. What does honesty require?

options.text: Waiting to see whether the customer complains
Asking a colleague to take over the case
Quietly correcting the record and saying nothing
Telling your manager so it can be put right

questions.hint: Errors should be reported and corrected as soon as possible.

questions.prompt: A customer asks a question you cannot answer. What does honesty require?

options.text: Telling them it is not the department's concern
Giving your best guess so the call stays short
Transferring the call without any explanation
Saying you will find out rather than guessing

questions.hint: Do not invent answers; check and come back.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with a case note that makes a call sound better than it was?

options.text: It does not give a truthful record of the facts
It reveals too much of the department's thinking
It was written by the wrong person
It was written after the call finished

questions.hint: Records must be accurate and truthful.

questions.prompt: Why is honesty important in a Civil Service job application?

options.text: Honest applicants are placed on a higher grade
The pre-employment checks test the information you give
False details matter only for senior roles
Only the interview is used to check the details in your application

questions.hint: Checks verify identity, history and convictions, so false information can end an offer.

questions.prompt: A customer asks about another person's claim. What is the honest and correct response?

options.text: Say you cannot discuss anyone else's information
Say that no such claim exists
Give a vague answer to avoid the question
Tell them a little detail so that they stop asking about it

questions.hint: Honesty does not mean sharing confidential facts or telling lies.

questions.prompt: Which officer is acting honestly?

options.text: One who leaves out a detail that makes them look bad
One who tells a customer what they want to hear
One who rounds up their hours on a timesheet
One who reports a payment error they made themselves

questions.hint: Reporting your own error is honest.

questions.prompt: Under the Code, who must civil servants not knowingly mislead?

options.text: Ministers, Parliament and others
Only the ministers they work for
Only members of the public
Only their line managers

questions.hint: The Code says do not deceive or knowingly mislead ministers, Parliament or others.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the honesty value?

options.text: All information is published at once
People can trust what the Civil Service tells them
Civil servants can avoid being criticised
Decisions can be taken more quickly by senior managers

questions.hint: Honesty builds trust in the Civil Service.

items.title: Objectivity: advice based on evidence (level 2)
items.body: Objectivity is the value of basing your advice and decisions on rigorous analysis of the evidence. That means looking at the facts, comparing the options and explaining your reasons, instead of relying on opinion, habit or what you would like to be true. The Civil Service Code says civil servants should provide information and advice, including advice to ministers, on the basis of the evidence, and should present options and facts accurately. They should take decisions on the merits of the case and take account of expert and professional advice. They must not ignore inconvenient facts or relevant considerations. Objectivity is useful at every grade. An Administrative Officer who checks a claim should look at the documents provided, apply the rules to them and record the reason for the decision. They should not decide because a customer is friendly or difficult, or because they have a hunch. A team leader who must choose between two ways of working should look at the figures on speed and accuracy. Objective decisions can be explained and defended later, and they are fair because the same facts lead to the same result for everyone. When a fact is not known, an objective person says so and does not pretend to be certain. They also separate what is known from what they think.

questions.prompt: What does objectivity mean when checking a claim?

options.text: Following your instinct about whether the customer is honest
Applying the rules to the documents and recording why
Passing every difficult claim to a colleague
Giving the benefit of the doubt to friendly callers

questions.hint: Objectivity uses evidence, not feelings.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of ignoring an inconvenient fact?

options.text: Asking an expert to review the draft
Checking a figure with a colleague before using it
Using an up-to-date official source for a statistic in a report
Leaving a figure out of a report because it spoils the case

questions.hint: Objectivity means including all relevant evidence.

questions.prompt: Why are objective decisions fair?

options.text: The same facts lead to the same result for everyone
They are always made faster than any other kind of decision
They always go in the customer's favour
They are never challenged by anyone

questions.hint: Consistent use of evidence treats people equally.

questions.prompt: A team leader must choose between two ways of working. What would be objective?

options.text: Following whoever argues the loudest
Copying the approach used in their last job
Comparing figures on speed and accuracy for each
Choosing the one most colleagues find comfortable

questions.hint: Evidence gives a fair comparison.

questions.prompt: What should an objective person do when a fact is not yet known?

options.text: Give a confident estimate and present it as fact
Leave the point out of the report altogether
Say clearly that it is not yet known
Hand the decision to a more senior person

questions.hint: Be clear about what is known and what is not.

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of objectivity in the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Taking account of expert and professional advice
Giving ministers only the good news about a project
Keeping decisions off the record
Choosing whichever option is quickest

questions.hint: The Code asks civil servants to take account of expert advice.

questions.prompt: Which of these decisions is NOT objective?

options.text: Recording the reason for the decision
Applying the correct rule to the facts
Checking all the documents that the customer supplied
Approving a claim because you like the customer

questions.hint: Personal feelings should not decide cases.

questions.prompt: What should advice to ministers contain?

options.text: Facts and options set out accurately
Only options the Opposition would back
Only the cheapest option available
Only the option the adviser prefers

questions.hint: Advice must present options and facts accurately.

items.title: Departments and agencies compared (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies
items.body: The Civil Service is made up of departments and agencies, and it helps to know how they differ. A ministerial department is led by a minister, usually the Secretary of State, who sets the direction of the department and answers for it in Parliament. Examples are the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice and the Department for Work and Pensions. A non-ministerial department has no minister in charge of the day-to-day running. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is a well-known example. It is led by a board and a chief executive, and it has a minister who answers for it in Parliament. An executive agency is part of a department. It carries out a specific job, and it has more freedom to decide how to do that job day to day. The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), part of the Department for Transport, is an example. Another is HM Passport Office, which belongs to the Home Office. The head of an agency is normally called the Chief Executive. The agency's staff are civil servants, and the Civil Service Code applies to them just as it does in the main department. Arm's length bodies are different again: they work independently of ministers on some matters. Because agencies are separate organisations, each one advertises its own jobs.

questions.prompt: Who leads a ministerial department?

options.text: A minister, usually a Secretary of State
A board of senior civil servants
The chief executive of its biggest agency
The Speaker of the House of Commons

questions.hint: Ministerial departments are headed by a minister.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a ministerial department?

options.text: Companies House
HM Passport Office
The Home Office
The DVLA

questions.hint: The Home Office is led by a Secretary of State; the others are agencies or bodies.

questions.prompt: What is an executive agency?

options.text: A committee of MPs that scrutinises the department's spending
A private company that competes with the department
A part of a department that carries out a specific job
A group of ministers who advise the Prime Minister

questions.hint: Agencies do a specific job within a parent department.

questions.prompt: Which department does HM Passport Office belong to?

options.text: The Ministry of Justice
The Home Office
The Department for Work and Pensions
The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office

questions.hint: HM Passport Office is part of the Home Office.

questions.prompt: What is the head of an executive agency normally called?

options.text: Permanent Secretary
Chief Executive
Secretary of State
Cabinet Secretary

questions.hint: Agencies are normally led by a Chief Executive.

questions.prompt: How does the Civil Service Code apply to agency staff?

options.text: Only to staff who work with ministers
In the same way as it does in the main department
Only in the first year of employment
Not at all, because agencies set their own values

questions.hint: Agency staff are civil servants and the Code covers them.

questions.prompt: Why is HMRC called a non-ministerial department?

options.text: A board and chief executive run it instead of a minister day to day
It does not employ civil servants directly
A private company runs it on behalf of the government
It has no connection with ministers and answers only to its own board

questions.hint: HMRC is led by a board and chief executive.

questions.prompt: Why search for agencies as well as departments on Civil Service Jobs?

options.text: Each agency may advertise its own vacancies
Departments never advertise AO jobs
Agencies are not part of the Civil Service
Agencies only employ staff at senior grades

questions.hint: Agencies are separate organisations that advertise their own jobs.

items.title: What operational delivery work looks like (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service functions and professions
items.body: Operational delivery is the largest group of jobs in the Civil Service, and it is where many Administrative Officers start. Operational delivery staff run public services and deal directly with customers. Different departments do this in different ways. In the Department for Work and Pensions, staff in Jobcentre Plus and benefit teams help people to claim Universal Credit and other benefits, check their claims and answer questions. In HM Revenue and Customs, staff answer calls about tax and tax credits, deal with letters and check tax returns. In the Home Office, staff process visa and passport applications. In the Ministry of Justice, staff work in courts, prisons and probation services. Operational delivery staff often follow set procedures and use computer systems to keep records. Their targets might include how quickly they answer calls, how long cases take, and how accurate the work is. The work can be busy and sometimes emotional, because customers may be anxious about money or personal problems. But it is also rewarding, because the work makes a real difference to people. Training is provided, and the skills gained, such as communication, accuracy and problem-solving, are useful in other parts of the Civil Service.

questions.prompt: Which work would an operational delivery AO in DWP most likely do?

options.text: Running practical driving tests for learner drivers and riders
Helping people claim Universal Credit and checking claims
Issuing patents to inventors
Collecting Corporation Tax from large companies

questions.hint: DWP staff help people with benefits such as Universal Credit.

questions.prompt: A caller wants to ask about their tax code. Whose operational staff would deal with it?

options.text: The Home Office
DVLA
HMRC
DWP

questions.hint: HMRC deals with tax, including tax codes.

questions.prompt: Which skill is useful across many operational delivery roles?

options.text: Speaking several foreign languages
Drafting new laws for Parliament
Communicating clearly and recording information accurately
Designing buildings and other large structures for departments

questions.hint: Communication and accuracy matter across the work.

questions.prompt: Why can operational delivery work be emotionally demanding?

options.text: Staff must make decisions with no guidance, training or rules
Ministers blame staff personally for every complaint
Customers may be anxious or upset about their circumstances
Staff work alone without any contact with colleagues

questions.hint: Customers dealing with money or personal problems can be worried.

questions.prompt: Which of these might be a target in operational delivery?

options.text: How many press releases the team writes
How many new policies the team proposes to ministers each month
How many ministers the team briefs each week
How quickly calls are answered and how accurate the work is

questions.hint: Targets often cover speed and accuracy.

questions.prompt: What is one benefit of starting in operational delivery?

options.text: It means never dealing with the public
Skills gained transfer to other parts of the Civil Service
It guarantees automatic promotion after the first full year
It leads straight into the Senior Civil Service

questions.hint: Skills such as communication and accuracy transfer.

questions.prompt: Where do operational staff usually record the details of a customer's case?

options.text: In an email sent to their own address
In a personal notebook kept at home
On a department computer system
In a spreadsheet on a personal laptop

questions.hint: Records belong on approved department systems.

questions.prompt: Which description fits Jobcentre Plus?

options.text: An HMRC service that helps individuals file their yearly tax returns
A Home Office service for visa applications
A DWP service that helps people find work and claim benefits
A Ministry of Justice service for probation

questions.hint: Jobcentre Plus is part of DWP.

items.title: Moving up from AO to EO and beyond (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service grades; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Moving up the Civil Service grades usually means taking on more responsibility, not just a bigger salary. An Administrative Officer (AO) normally works on set tasks under supervision, following procedures and dealing with cases or enquiries. An Executive Officer (EO) is the next grade. EOs often handle more complex cases, check the work of others, look after a small team or take the lead on a piece of work. A Higher Executive Officer (HEO) takes on larger responsibilities, such as managing a larger team, running a project or giving advice on policy. A Senior Executive Officer (SEO) manages managers or leads a more complex area. Grade 7 and Grade 6 are senior management and professional grades, and above them the Senior Civil Service leads whole parts of a department. To move up, a person usually applies for a role at the next grade when it is advertised. They are assessed on their behaviours and experience against the requirements of that grade. Some departments also have temporary promotion, which means doing a higher-grade job for a set time to gain experience. Good performance, learning new skills and finding opportunities to help with extra tasks all strengthen your case. You should talk to your line manager about your goals.

questions.prompt: What does an EO normally do that an AO may not?

options.text: Set policy for the whole department and sign off its budget
Lead a government department as its head
Look after a small team or handle more complex cases
Advise the Prime Minister directly

questions.hint: EOs take on more responsibility, such as small teams and complex cases.

questions.prompt: Which grade is directly above Higher Executive Officer?

options.text: Grade 7
Grade 6
Executive Officer
Senior Executive Officer

questions.hint: The order is AO, EO, HEO, SEO, Grade 7, Grade 6.

questions.prompt: How do people usually move up a grade?

options.text: By passing a test on the Civil Service Code
By waiting for an automatic promotion after each year of service
By applying for a role at the next grade when it is advertised
By being nominated by the Permanent Secretary

questions.hint: Promotion usually means applying and being assessed.

questions.prompt: What is temporary promotion?

options.text: A short leave of absence on full pay
A pay rise that lasts for a single month and then ends automatically
A transfer to another department for a year
Doing a higher-grade job for a set time to gain experience

questions.hint: Temporary promotion gives experience of a higher grade.

questions.prompt: On what are people assessed when they apply for the next grade?

options.text: Their behaviours and experience against the grade's requirements
Their age and length of service in the department and their sickness record
Their attendance record alone
Their qualifications and nothing else

questions.hint: Assessment is against the requirements of the role.

questions.prompt: What does a Senior Executive Officer usually manage?

options.text: Managers or a more complex area of work
Only a single team of AOs
The department's whole budget
An entire government department

questions.hint: SEOs usually manage managers or complex work.

questions.prompt: Which action could strengthen your case for promotion?

options.text: Keeping quiet about your achievements so far
Avoiding contact with senior colleagues
Taking on extra tasks and learning new skills
Staying with exactly the same tasks for many years

questions.hint: Showing growth strengthens an application.

questions.prompt: Which meeting is the best place to discuss your career goals?

options.text: A parliamentary select committee session
A regular one-to-one with your line manager
An exit interview when you leave
A Civil Service Commission hearing about your application

questions.hint: One-to-ones are where managers support development.

items.title: Joining with no qualifications (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service apprenticeships; Success Profiles
items.body: You do not need a degree or other formal qualifications for many Civil Service jobs. At AA and AO level, adverts usually ask you to show that you have the right skills, behaviours and experience. The Civil Service uses a framework called Success Profiles to assess candidates fairly. It looks at five things: behaviours, strengths, experience, ability and technical skills. A particular advert uses only some of these. Experience can come from paid work, volunteering or caring for a family member. You do not need to have worked in an office before. Some adverts ask for GCSEs in English and maths, but many do not, and the advert will say. An apprenticeship is another way in. Apprentices work and earn a wage while studying towards a qualification, and the Civil Service offers apprenticeships in subjects such as business administration, customer service, digital skills and finance. The Fast Stream is a graduate programme that needs a degree, so it is not the usual route for an AO. If you are not sure whether you qualify, read the person specification in the advert. It lists the essential criteria. If you meet those, you can apply. If you need an adjustment because of a disability, you can ask for one.

questions.prompt: What do AO adverts usually ask you to show?

options.text: Previous work in a government office
The right skills, behaviours and experience
A degree in public administration or a similar subject
A reference from a former civil servant

questions.hint: Many adverts test skills rather than qualifications.

questions.prompt: How many elements make up the Success Profiles framework?

options.text: Seven
Three
Five
Nine

questions.hint: Success Profiles has five elements.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the Success Profiles elements?

options.text: Loyalty
Availability
Seniority
Strengths

questions.hint: The elements are behaviours, strengths, experience, ability and technical.

questions.prompt: Which of these could count as experience in an application?

options.text: Only paid jobs in an office
Volunteering or caring for a family member
Only time spent in a government department
Only completed apprenticeships

questions.hint: Experience can be paid or unpaid.

questions.prompt: What does an apprentice do?

options.text: Works and earns a wage while studying for a qualification
Completes a degree before starting work
Works unpaid for a year before being hired
Studies full time at college and receives a maintenance grant

questions.hint: Apprenticeships combine paid work with study.

questions.prompt: Which scheme is the Civil Service graduate programme?

options.text: Jobcentre Plus
The Disability Confident scheme
The Fast Stream
A Civil Service apprenticeship

items.title: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (level 2)
items.body: The UK has four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own devolved government, which makes decisions on some matters for that nation, such as health or education. Devolved means that some powers have been passed down from the UK Parliament. The Scottish Government and the Welsh Government employ civil servants who work for the devolved ministers. They are part of the UK Civil Service and the Civil Service Code applies to them. Northern Ireland is different, because it has its own separate Civil Service, called the Northern Ireland Civil Service (NICS). It has its own recruitment website and its own rules, although it is based on similar principles. The UK government, in Westminster, remains responsible for matters that are not devolved, such as defence and foreign affairs. UK government departments, such as DWP and HMRC, have offices in all four nations. When you search for jobs, check whether an advert is for the UK Civil Service, the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government or the NICS. Each recruits through its own pages, and the application process, though similar, may differ in detail. Welsh language skills are sometimes needed for jobs in Wales.

items.title: Merit and the Civil Service Commission (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; GOV.UK
items.body: The Civil Service Commission is an independent body set up to protect the principle that civil servants are appointed on merit after fair and open competition. It was established in its present form by law, in the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. Its job is to oversee recruitment and to make sure the Recruitment Principles are followed. The Commission is separate from the government, which means ministers cannot tell it what to say. This independence lets it check departments without fear or favour. The Commissioners are appointed by the Crown and include the First Civil Service Commissioner. The Commission has a second role. Under the Civil Service Code, a civil servant who has raised a concern inside their department and is not satisfied with the response can take the matter to the Commission. The Commission can investigate and report. The Commission also publishes guidance on recruitment and checks departments' compliance. Exceptions to open competition are allowed in limited cases, for example short-term appointments or placements for disabled people, but they must be reported. Applicants who believe the rules were not followed can complain, first to the department and then, if that fails, to the Commission.

items.title: Arm's length bodies (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies
items.body: Some organisations that do public work are not departments or agencies. They are called arm's length bodies. They work at a distance from ministers on certain matters, but they are still funded by the public and linked to a government department that is called their sponsor. Examples include the Environment Agency, which protects the environment in England and is sponsored by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), and the Care Quality Commission, which inspects health and social care services in England and is sponsored by the Department of Health and Social Care. Arts Council England, which funds the arts, is another. The Health and Safety Executive, which regulates workplace safety, is sponsored by the Department for Work and Pensions. Some of these bodies, such as the Environment Agency, employ staff who are not civil servants. Others have their own employment rules. When you apply to one of them, the advert will say whether the job is in the Civil Service. This matters because Civil Service rules, such as the Civil Service Code, apply only to civil servants. Many arm's length bodies still advertise on Civil Service Jobs, so you will see them in your search results. Read the advert to see who the employer is and what the terms are.

items.title: Raising a concern under the Code (level 2)
items.body: The Civil Service Code does not only describe good behaviour. It also tells civil servants what to do if they are asked to do something wrong or if they see something that worries them. This is often called raising a concern. First, you can talk to your line manager or another manager in the department. Most problems are resolved at this stage. If you do not want to go to your line manager, you can go to someone else in the management chain. Each department also has a nominated officer, who is a person you can talk to in confidence. Confidence means they will not share what you say without good reason. A department may also have an independent helpline. If you have done all this and are still concerned, you may take the matter to the Civil Service Commission, which is independent of departments. The Code says that civil servants should report evidence of criminal or unlawful activity to the police or other appropriate authorities. Civil servants who raise concerns in good faith are protected from unfair treatment by law, through the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998. Raising a concern is not disloyal: it is part of upholding the Code and protecting the public.

items.title: More government departments and Whitehall (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies
items.body: Besides the departments that deal most with the public, several others shape how government works. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) is responsible for UK foreign policy, diplomacy and the network of embassies and consulates around the world. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) covers farming, food and the environment. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) covers areas such as the arts, museums, broadcasting and sport. The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) sets national policy for health and adult social care in England. The NHS delivers care, and most NHS staff are not civil servants. HM Treasury sets tax and spending plans, while HMRC is the department that collects the tax. The Cabinet Office supports the Prime Minister and the Cabinet and helps departments work together. The Department for Transport (DfT) has agencies such as the DVLA and the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. Many of these departments have their headquarters in or near Whitehall, a street in central London. Journalists often use the word Whitehall to mean the central government departments and their civil servants. Remember that many departments have offices across the UK, so working for them does not mean you must move to London.
